title: Words Shakespeare Gave Us
objective: After this level you can explain why so many everyday words and phrases are first recorded in Shakespeare, and what "first recorded" means.
summary: Many words and phrases, like the green-eyed monster, are first recorded in Shakespeare. That means the earliest written use found so far, not proof he coined them: earlier uses keep turning up.

cards.headline: Feeling jealous? You may be quoting Iago.
cards.body: In Othello, Iago warns: "beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the green-ey'd monster". People still call jealousy the green-eyed monster. Like "sour grapes" from Aesop's fable in Level 2, a phrase has escaped its story and moved into everyday speech.

cards.headline: A mountain of firsts
cards.body: Shakespeare's works give the first recorded use of a great many English words. He may have made plenty of them himself, by combining words, turning nouns into verbs, or adding prefixes and suffixes. He was the first writer on record, for instance, to use partner, property and scissor as verbs. The words already existed; he put them to new work.

cards.headline: First recorded isn't first said
cards.body: Careful, though. A word's earliest known use means the earliest evidence found so far, not the day it was invented. The Oxford English Dictionary's original editors and hundreds of volunteer readers recorded Shakespeare's language in more detail than any other writer's, so his uses were the ones they found. Look where they looked less, and older uses turn up: assassination, in Macbeth, appears in a 1572 letter by the diplomat Sir Thomas Smith.

mascot.line: Keep this: first recorded means the oldest example found so far. A new search can always push the date back.

cards.headline: Words that wander
cards.body: Some phrases survive while their meaning moves. In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio jokes about a "wild-goose chase": a horse race in which the leader chose any course and the others had to follow. Today a wild-goose chase means a fruitless search. The words stayed; the race was forgotten.

cards.headline: Shakespeare's words: dated
learned: He turned nouns like partner into verbs
First recorded means earliest found so far

questions.prompt: In Othello, Iago calls _____ "the green-ey'd monster".

options.label: greed
options.rationale: Iago is warning about something else.

questions.explanation: Iago warns, "beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the green-ey'd monster", and jealousy is still called that today.

questions.prompt: Why are so many English words first recorded in Shakespeare?

options.label: Dictionary readers combed his works more closely than anyone else's
His were the only English books of his time to survive
options.rationale: Plenty survive; a 1572 letter held an older use.

options.label: A law required new words to appear in plays first
Dictionaries accept words only from poets
options.rationale: Letters and legal papers count too.

questions.explanation: The OED's editors and volunteer readers recorded Shakespeare's language in more detail than any other writer's, so his uses were found first.

questions.prompt: "Sour grapes" comes from Aesop's fable in Level 2. What do sour grapes and the green-eyed monster have in common?

options.label: Both were coined by Shakespeare
options.rationale: Sour grapes comes from Aesop's fable.

options.label: Both describe jealousy
options.rationale: Sour grapes means scorning what you can't have.

options.label: Both first appeared in Latin
options.rationale: Nothing in either level says so.

options.label: Both phrases escaped from a story into everyday speech

questions.explanation: A fox's excuse and Iago's warning both left their stories behind and became everyday phrases.
